Title:Understanding and Mitigating Inference-Time Overreliance Using Agentic Memory
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Agentic memory allows LLM agents to reuse past experience, yet retrieved memories can also distort inference even when they are benign, correctly stored, and appropriately retrieved. We study this failure mode, which we call memory over-reliance. Across benchmarks and memory architectures, we find that memory is useful when past experience transfers to the current task, but can become misleading when only part of the evidence transfers. Failures are strongest under partial query-memory overlap, a pattern further confirmed by controlled experiments thatvary the amount of overlapping evidence. Motivated by this finding, we propose MEMTRIM, a plug-and-play framework that indexes memory evidence at write time and controls its reuse at read time. MEMTRIM removes repeated or conflicting evidence while preserving useful memory-specific information, requires no retraining, and applies to both embedding-based and structured memory this http URL show that MEMTRIM reduces memory overreliance while preserving the benefits of useful memory across models and memory settings.

report.summary: New research identifies inference-time memory over-reliance in LLM agents and proposes MEMTRIM, a plug-and-play method that curbs misleading retrieved memories without retraining.
report.background: Agentic memory has become a core ingredient in LLM agents. Systems store past interactions, documents, tool outputs, and user preferences, then retrieve relevant items to condition future responses. This reuse promises personalization, continuity, and fewer repeated mistakes. Much of the industry assumes that better storage and retrieval automatically improve agent performance, driving adoption of vector databases, memory APIs, and persistent agent frameworks. However, retrieval-augmented and memory-augmented models can over-weight context that is only superficially relevant. The paper studies this overlooked failure mode: benign, correctly stored, and appropriately retrieved memories can still distort inference. It finds failures are strongest under partial query-memory overlap, when only part of the past evidence applies. Motivated by controlled experiments, the authors propose MEMTRIM, a lightweight framework for indexing evidence at write time and controlling reuse at read time without retraining.
key_points: The paper names a failure mode called memory over-reliance: an LLM agent can be misled by retrieved memories even when those memories are benign, correctly stored, and appropriately retrieved. The effect is strongest when a query only partially overlaps with stored experience, so some evidence transfers but not all.

Through benchmarks and controlled experiments, the authors show memory helps when past experience truly transfers, but becomes misleading under partial evidence overlap. Varying the amount of overlapping evidence confirms the pattern, suggesting the problem is structural to how agents reuse memory rather than a rare data corruption issue.

MEMTRIM is a plug-and-play framework that indexes memory evidence at write time and controls reuse at read time. It removes repeated or conflicting evidence while preserving useful memory-specific information. It requires no retraining and works with both embedding-based and structured memory systems.

Across models and memory settings, MEMTRIM reduces memory over-reliance while preserving the benefits of useful memory. The results imply agent builders should treat memory as evidence to be weighed, not context to be blindly injected, and should evaluate systems under partial query-memory overlap.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the findings challenge the 'more memory is better' assumption underpinning many agent platforms. Memory over-reliance is a subtle reliability risk: agents can sound confident while being anchored to partially relevant past experience. MEMTRIM's no-retraining, plug-and-play design could make memory hygiene a standard middleware layer in agent stacks. Developers should test memory systems beyond retrieval accuracy, adding partial-overlap evaluations and read-time gating. Regular users may see more consistent assistants that are less likely to repeat stale or half-relevant personalization, though overly aggressive filtering could reduce useful continuity if not tuned. Overall, the work shifts attention from memory capacity to memory evidence control.
report.tools: To follow up, watch the MEMTRIM reference implementation if released with the arXiv paper, plus open agent-memory projects such as Letta/MemGPT, Mem0, Zep, Cognee, and the memory modules in LangChain and LlamaIndex. For evaluation, consider retrieval and agent-memory test suites like RAGAS and TruLens. These tools let developers experiment with write-time indexing, read-time filtering, and partial-overlap stress tests in their own agents.
